_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Granted, [if you say] Rabbi Meir [spoke] as a stringency: that he deems one liable even in more than the time it takes to eat a peras [half-loaf]; this is why the Rabbis say to him: he is never liable in more than the time it takes to eat a peras, but only if his time spent eating them is the measure of a peras.
rashi:a2.1: But if you say Rabbi Meir [spoke] as a leniency: he says that even within the time it takes to eat a peras it does not combine if he interrupted in between, and the Rabbis wish to be stringent; why [say] “unless he expends”? They should have said: If he expended the time it takes to eat a peras he is liable, which implies: even though he interrupted.
rashi:a3.1: With fats and with a carcass: he ate two half olive-bulks of forbidden fat or of an animal carcass.
rashi:a3.2: Impure foods: their measure for disqualifying the body is a half-peras [the quarter-loaf of the translation].
rashi:a3.3: And impure liquids: disqualify the body with a quarter[-log].
rashi:a3.4: Even the entire day: he took [that long] eating the half-peras, provided that he eats each olive-bulk of it within the time it takes to eat a peras.
rashi:a7.1: They did not permit one who eats less than the measure to descend and immerse: since he does not need immersion; and below [the Gemara] explains why it should matter to him.
rashi:a7.2: They permitted her, etc.: this is explained below.
rashi:a9.1: One who touched one impure through a corpse: [they permitted it] to a woman who touched one impure through a corpse.
rashi:a10.1: The refutation of Ravnai: who said: each olive-bulk, etc.
rashi:a14.1: He becomes impure from the milk: for granted, from the contact, when she touched him, her son does not become impure, since she, having touched one impure through a corpse, is first-degree, and people and vessels become impure only from a primary source of impurity. Rather, he becomes impure from the milk, for one who eats a half-peras of impure foods, his body is disqualified.
rashi:a15.1: And if you say it was not rendered susceptible: this milk, and so it is not impure; for milk does not have the status of a liquid, since a liquid that comes [to be used] as food is like food, [as stated] in tractate Shabbat, in the chapter Ḥavit Shenishbera (144b); therefore it needs to be rendered susceptible.
rashi:a15.2: But it was rendered susceptible by the drop smeared on the nipple: that is, by the drop with which the nipple is smeared, for that certainly renders susceptible the rest of the milk that comes out that way, since it does not stand to be eaten by the infant.
rashi:a15.3: That he nursed with one strong [suck]: with force.
rashi:a16.1: The mouth of the infant that is full of milk: therefore it is impossible that there not be a drop smeared on the nipple.
rashi:a16.2: And furthermore: milk does not have the status of food [or of a liquid], for it is one of the woman’s springs, like her saliva and her urine, of which we say below that they impart severe impurity in any amount, since it is like one of her limbs.
rashi:a17.1: Whether to the satisfaction: of the infant, or not to the satisfaction, when he does not want to nurse; and it teaches that it imparts impurity. And if it had the status of food, why does it impart impurity not to satisfaction? It has not been properly rendered susceptible, for we require [a case] like “if water be put” (Leviticus 11:38), where it is agreeable to him.
rashi:a18.1: [A marginal gloss (gilyon), printed with Rashi, begins here.] Rava said: There are two refutations of the matter, etc.: that is, we see that at times the infant does not nurse with force and leaves a drop smeared on the nipple.
rashi:a18.2: And furthermore, the place of the milk is a spring: and so it is like one of her limbs, and it will become impure without being rendered susceptible, like her saliva.
rashi:a18.3: Not to the satisfaction: what is it? That it is not agreeable to the infant; then the milk is not rendered susceptible by the drop smeared on the nipple, since it came out not to the infant’s satisfaction, for we require [a case] like “if water be put”; and yet it teaches that it becomes impure, even though it was not rendered susceptible. Evidently it is a spring; so why is her son pure?
rashi:a19.1: Rather, Rava said, etc.: rather, the place of the milk is not a spring, and it needs to be rendered susceptible; but where it is not agreeable to him it is pure, since it was not rendered susceptible; and from now on he can explain it [the mishna] as referring to “not to the satisfaction.” Thus far the marginal gloss.
rashi:a19.2: The measure: a quarter[-log]; and if it is [counted as] food, a half-peras. It is uncertain whether he nursed the measure, and he is pure. For this milk, even though it is a spring, does not impart impurity in any amount, since she herself does not impart impurity by contact, as she is first-degree; therefore her milk has only the impurity of other liquids.
rashi:a21.1: The woman whose milk dripped, etc.: when she is menstruating. And if it is a spring, it becomes impure in any amount, like one of her limbs; so why does it need to be rendered susceptible?
rashi:a22.1: And if you say, etc., but isn’t it taught: explicitly, that it is not a spring.
rashi:a22.2: Ill-smelling pus: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b1.1: His saliva, in any amount: as it is written: “And if the zav spits upon one who is pure” (Leviticus 15:8); and his discharge and his urine we derive from his saliva, in tractate Nidda, in the chapter Dam HaNidda (Nidda 55a).
rashi:b5.1: And remained the time it takes to eat a peras (12b): implies that he remained in the Temple; and that is what [the Gemara] asks in the Gemara: Why do I need him to remain, that it teaches “and remained”?
rashi:b7.1: Until forty days: it is sweet and does not intoxicate.
rashi:b8.1: They are warned about it in any amount and from its press: but he is not [liable] to death until he drinks a quarter[-log] forty days old.
rashi:b11.1: With regard to what do they disagree: the first tanna and Rabbi Yehuda.
rashi:b11.2: [We learn] “intoxicating drink,” “intoxicating drink” from a nazirite.
rashi:b13.1: A dried fig of Ke’ila [de’veila ke’ilit]: [Ke’ila is] a place.
rashi:b14.1: Had a vow regarding his wife: not to derive benefit from her.
rashi:b14.2: He came before Rav Ashi: after eating and drinking.
rashi:b14.3: Would not place a disseminator over himself: to expound in the public lecture.
rashi:b14.4: From one Festival day to the next: after he had held the Festival rejoicing, eating and drinking, until the next day, because of drunkenness.
rashi:b15.1: With more than a quarter[-log]: even though he puts water in it, it intoxicates; and I drank more than a quarter[-log].
rashi:b16.1: And that you may differentiate: “Drink no wine nor intoxicating drink…when you go into the Tent of Meeting…and that you may differentiate”: and when you come to differentiate between the sacred and the common, likewise do not drink wine and intoxicating drink.
rashi:b16.2: Values and valuations and consecrations: that those who have drunk wine are forbidden to appraise them for the owners so that they can redeem them, lest they not appraise them properly.
rashi:b17.1: The ruling: on what is forbidden and permitted; those who have drunk wine are forbidden [to give] it.
rashi:b17.2: Expositions: that are expounded in the public lecture; they are forbidden to those who have drunk wine, since they contain rulings.
rashi:b18.1: The verse states: “And that you may instruct”: to exclude Mishna, since one does not rule on halakha from the Mishna; therefore those who have drunk wine are permitted to study it.
rashi:b18.2: Rabbi Yosei [so Rashi’s heading; the daf reads Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda] says: One might have thought that even Talmud: would be forbidden to study; the verse states “and that you may instruct”: I forbade only ruling on halakha in practice.
rashi:b19.1: Those who have drunk wine may rule: that a creeping animal is impure and a frog pure, and we are not concerned, for it is known to all.
rashi:b19.2: Let us say it is Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda [so Rashi’s heading]: who said that those who have drunk wine are permitted [to study] Talmud, and it is impossible that one will not understand and rule from it; and not the Rabbis, who forbade even studying Talmud, and all the more so any ruling.
rashi:b20.1: But Rav would not place, etc.: and why would he not expound in the public lecture? Since Talmud is permitted, all the more so expositions.
rashi:b20.2: It is not possible without a ruling: for everyone asks him.
rashi:b21.1: Mishna. Four sin offerings: one because he ate sacred [meat] while impure, one because of forbidden fat, one because of notar, and one because of Yom Kippur.
rashi:b21.2: And a guilt offering: for misuse [of consecrated property].
rashi:b22.1: It is not of the same category: for this liability is not because of eating.
tosafot:a4.1: And that he ate an olive-bulk within the time it takes to eat a peras: meaning that he ate each olive-bulk of the half-peras within the time it takes to eat a peras, even though he paused between one olive-bulk and the next. And we do not say that the half-peras that disqualifies the body is like the olive-bulk of forbidden fat or of a carcass, so that he would need to eat the whole half-peras within the time it takes to eat a peras.
tosafot:a7.1: They permitted a pregnant woman to eat less than the measure due to the danger: And if you say: even without danger [it is permitted], as we say (Tohorot 2:3): “And the third[-degree] may be eaten in a stew of teruma mixture”; and likewise in the first chapter of Ḥullin (2b) it says: “An impure person [slaughtering] non-sacred food: what is the point of saying it?” even though the non-sacred food is [thereby] impure. One may say: here it deals with eating teruma afterward; but where she will not eat teruma, even the full measure [is permitted]. And if you say: what is [the Gemara’s] objection, “due to the danger, let her eat even a lot”? One may say: at times she has nothing but teruma.
tosafot:a7.2: Due to the danger: even according to Reish Lakish, [who holds] that a half-measure is permitted by Torah law, it is in any case forbidden by rabbinic law, and in a place of danger they permitted it.
tosafot:a14.1: Since he nursed, he became impure from the milk, etc.: [for] it was rendered susceptible by the drop smeared on the nipple, since that drop is not destined to be nursed by the infant, and it is a liquid. And if you say: but it says in the chapter Kol Sha’a (Pesaḥim 33b): “Once he squeezed it, its measure decreased,” and the Ri explained [it as] referring to rendering susceptible, that less than the measure does not receive susceptibility; and here, in the infant’s mouth, there is not an egg-bulk of milk. One may say: by rabbinic law it does not require an egg-bulk, and there it is by Torah law.
tosafot:a14.2: Why is her son pure: since he nursed of the milk, he became impure from the milk and his body is disqualified through the impurity of the body.
tosafot:a16.1: In brief: Rava said: There are two refutations…and furthermore, the place of the milk is a spring. Since it is a spring and imparts impurity like her saliva, we cannot say that the milk at the nipple, because it is designated for the infant, is food and loses the name “liquid,” for that would mean it is not a spring and does not impart impurity in a zava like her saliva; and if so [it is a spring], why does it need to be rendered susceptible? At this stage Rava mistakenly thinks that since it gathers and comes out like saliva it counts as a spring, even though it is not reabsorbed. Rava’s source is the mishna “a woman’s milk renders susceptible to satisfaction and not to satisfaction”: so it is a liquid by Torah law and a spring, like a zava’s; were it not a spring it would render susceptible only to satisfaction, like an animal’s milk; and even though it is more stringent than an animal’s milk with regard to the blood of its wound, as in the latter clause of that mishna, still, were it not a spring it would not render susceptible not to satisfaction. That is the approach of the Ri. Rashi explained that it is one of the woman’s springs, like her saliva and urine, which impart severe impurity in any amount, like one of her limbs. Tosafot find this difficult: here the case is a woman [impure through contact with] one impure through a corpse, who has no springs [of impurity]; what does “like one of her limbs” mean, when a menstruating woman herself does not impart impurity through her limbs; and her saliva and urine need a verse and do not come from this reasoning. Therefore it seems as Tosafot explained. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a16.2: And furthermore, the place of the milk is a spring: from here [we learn] that liquids that have the status of a spring render susceptible even not to satisfaction, and even when they come from a pure person; for the mishna deals with the milk of a pure woman, parallel to an animal’s milk. For if [it dealt] with an impure woman, why specify that it has the status of a spring? All impure liquids render susceptible, as we learned in Tohorot. And the reason is: since it imparts impurity not to satisfaction, it also renders susceptible not to satisfaction. It seems, however, that this applies only to impure [liquids] that come from the body; but liquids that became impure through a creeping animal have the law of pure liquids.
tosafot:b1.1: And a woman’s milk imparts the impurity of liquids with a quarter[-log]: And if you say: since it is a liquid by Torah law, as is implied in the chapter Dam HaNidda (Nidda 55b), which says [this of] the tears of his eye, as it is written: “And given them tears to drink in great measure” (Psalms 80:6), and of milk, as it is written: “And she opened the flask of milk and gave him drink” (Judges 4:19), then let it impart impurity in any amount, like other liquids. [That liquids impart impurity in any amount] is implied in the first chapter of Pesaḥim (14a), which says [the case is] where there is liquid with the meat, and it is not usual for a quarter[-log] of water to stick to meat; and also in the first chapter there (17b), which says of the liquids of the slaughterhouse: this was said only of a quarter[-log], which is fit for immersing needles and hooks, but not of less than a quarter[-log]; and also in the chapter Elu Devarim (Berakhot 52a), which says: one washes the hands and afterward mixes the cup, lest the liquids on the back of the cup become impure because of the hands and in turn render the cup impure, and it is not usual for a quarter[-log] to stick to the sides of a cup. Therefore it seems right to say that these are only rabbinic, and that is why a quarter[-log] is required, and the verse that is cited is a mere support.
tosafot:b5.1: He ate impure foods, etc.: Rashi explained that this does not refer to “entered the Temple,” for one is not liable for entering the Temple because of eating impure foods, even if they became impure through a corpse, since they do not become primary sources of impurity, as they have no purification in a ritual bath. And it seems that it deals with one who ate the carcass of a kosher bird and drank impure liquids, such as the blood of a creeping animal, which imparts impurity like its flesh, and entered the Temple.
tosafot:b5.2: And entered the Temple: meaning, and performed the service; but for entering without service one is not liable; and so they explained in the Torat Kohanim.
tosafot:b13.1: And entered the Temple and served: for he is liable only at the time of service, as it is derived at its end from the sanctification of the hands and feet. The Halakhot Gedolot [rules]: a priest who drank wine and lifted his hands [for the Priestly Blessing] is disqualified, and its measure is a quarter[-log], as we say: one who drank a quarter[-log] of wine should not pray; for prayer requires intention, and presumably the Priestly Blessing does not require more intention than prayer.
tosafot:b13.2: Rav said: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer [so Tosafot’s heading; the daf reads Rabbi Elazar]: And if you say: but Rav said (Ketubot 10b): One who ate dates should not issue rulings? One may say: there it is by rabbinic law, but by Torah law it is wine specifically.
tosafot:b21.1: Four sin offerings and one guilt offering: And if you say: why does it not count five, for example where he swore that he would not eat it and then ate it? One may say: it does not teach something that is subject to dissolution [by a sage]. And as for consecrated items, which it does teach even though they are subject to dissolution: in any case, now that they have been slaughtered and their blood sprinkled properly, they are no longer subject to dissolution. But one cannot say that it deals with a firstborn, for it says in the Gemara: “He consecrated it; since a prohibition was added,” etc.; and if it dealt with a firstborn it would not say “he consecrated it,” for it is sanctified by opening the womb.
tosafot:b21.2: And one guilt offering: as for the fact that he is liable to a guilt offering for misuse because of notar, even though it is worth nothing, while we say in the chapter Kol Sha’a (Pesaḥim 29a) that one who eats consecrated leavened bread during the Festival has not committed misuse: there it is a case of monetary sanctity, on which the sanctity of the body did not descend, and once it became forbidden for benefit it is not worth a peruta, and he did not benefit from consecrated property worth a peruta.
gershom:a1.1: [An editor’s marker notes that what precedes belongs to 12b.] Granted, if you say Rabbi Meir [spoke] as a stringency: he says that even if his eating extends the entire day he is liable; this is why the Rabbis respond to him: unless he expends the time it takes to eat a peras, and no more.
gershom:a2.1: But if you say: that he says it as a leniency, that since he interrupted in between he is exempt even though he did not expend more than the time it takes to eat a peras, then it should have taught: “And the Rabbis say: If he expended,” which would imply: if he expended the time it takes to eat a peras, even though he interrupted, he is liable.
gershom:a3.1: Rather, from the fact that it teaches “And the Rabbis say: Unless he expends,” conclude from it that Rabbi Meir spoke as a stringency; conclude from it.
gershom:a4.1: With fats and with a carcass: whose measure is an olive-bulk each, unless he expends on eating it the time it takes to eat a peras, and no more.
gershom:a5.1: But [if] he ate impure foods that touched a creeping animal or a zav, whose measure of eating to disqualify his body from teruma is a half-peras, or drank impure liquids, whose measure of drinking to disqualify is a quarter[-log]: even the entire day, within the time it takes to eat a peras.
gershom:a6.1: What is he saying? “Even the entire day,” and then he says “within the time it takes to eat a peras” and no more.
gershom:a7.1: This is what he is saying: even the entire day: [if] he drew out [the eating of] that half-peras of impure foods, it counts as [one] eating,
gershom:a8.1: provided that he ate each olive-bulk of that half-peras within the time it takes to eat a peras, and did not spend longer over it.
gershom:a9.1: What, is it not that he ate the half-peras: all of it within the time it takes to eat a peras? And [this would be] a refutation of Rav Pappa, who explains Ravnai’s statement.
gershom:a10.1: No, where he ate each olive-bulk of it within the time it takes to eat a peras.
gershom:a11.1: They did not permit one who eats less than the measure, etc., and they permitted a pregnant woman, etc., and they permitted one who touched one impure through a corpse, etc.: all of these it explains below.
gershom:a12.1: The Master said: They did not permit one who eats, etc. What is he saying? This is what he is saying: [if] he ate less than the measure, half the measure of impurity, they did not permit him to descend and immerse when he eats that half-measure. For if he descended and immersed and ascended, and afterward ate a half-measure and completed the first half-measure, they combine even though he immersed, and he must immerse now. And if they had permitted him to immerse immediately when he ate the first half-measure, then since he immersed and ascended and then completed it, he would come to say: My first immersion, which I performed in the interim, was effective for me, so they do not combine and I am not required to immerse now. And he does not know that since he completed it after he ascended, the immersion did not count for him and they combine; and immersion counts only at the end, for the last immersion, after the prohibition, is the essential one.
gershom:a13.1: They permitted a pregnant woman who smelled [food] on Yom Kippur to eat little by little, less than the measure of a date, due to the danger that she might miscarry.
gershom:a14.1: Even a lot: let her eat more than the measure, until she is revived.
gershom:a15.1: Rav Pappa said: This is what it teaches: she should eat less than the measure each time, little by little, even a lot, for it is a mitzva to alter [the manner of eating] so that she does not eat a full measure at once.
gershom:a16.1: It teaches: they permitted one who touched one impure through a corpse: a woman who touched one impure through a corpse, who is a first-degree derivative, [they permitted] to nurse her son, and her son is pure, so that he does not render sacred food or teruma impure by touching. What is the reason? She does not render her son impure by touching, since she is a derivative of impurity, and a derivative of impurity does not render a person impure. And her milk does not render him impure either, for even though it is a liquid, since it is an infant’s food we say: a liquid that comes [to be used] as food is like food, as we learned: One may milk [an animal] on a Festival into a pot, but not into a bowl; for in a pot one makes food, and we say a liquid that comes [to be used] as food is food, like food that was separated [from its source]; but not into a bowl, for a bowl is like a cup, and sometimes liquids are put in it; therefore one may not milk into it, for [the milk] would be newly created [nolad].
gershom:a17.1: And [the Gemara] asks: why is her son pure? Since he nursed milk, he became impure from the milk, for that is impure food.
gershom:a18.1: And if you say it was not rendered susceptible: this milk, which comes entirely [to be used] as food, and food renders a person impure only by way of being rendered susceptible,
gershom:a19.1: let it be rendered susceptible by the drop smeared on the nipple: [a word in parentheses in the printed text is unclear here] the first milk that the child sucks is not entirely drawn from the nipple, but some of it remains on the nipple, and through that drop the infant nurses all the rest of the milk; and when he stops nursing, that drop remains on the nipple. So let the rest of the milk, which is food, be rendered susceptible by that smeared drop, which is not food, and let the milk be impure and the infant be impure; so why is her son pure?
gershom:a20.1: Rav Naḥman said: For example, where the infant nursed with one strong [suck]: with one forceful suck, and did not leave a smeared drop, for he nursed it all, and the milk was not rendered susceptible by that drop; therefore her son is pure.
gershom:a21.1: There are two refutations of the matter: one, that we see the infant’s mouth full of milk when he stops nursing; evidently it is impossible for it to be with one strong suck such that no drop remains on the nipple, and through that [drop] the milk is rendered susceptible, and the milk and the child are impure.
gershom:a22.1: And furthermore, the place of the milk is a spring: that is, we do not regard it as gathered in it and deposited there; rather it is a spring, like one of her limbs and her springs, as it says: nine liquids with regard to a zav, etc. And since it is a spring, let her son be impure. And from where do we [know] that it is a spring? For we learned: A woman’s milk imparts impurity whether to satisfaction, where the woman is agreeable, having given it importance, or not to satisfaction, even though neither the woman nor the infant is agreeable to it; and it teaches that it becomes impure. Evidently it is a spring; so why is her son pure?
gershom:a23.1: This is the reason: for it is a double uncertainty: uncertain whether he nursed the measure of a quarter[-log], which imparts impurity; or, even if he nursed a quarter[-log], uncertain whether he nursed it within the time it takes to eat a peras or uncertain [whether] in more; therefore her son is pure.
gershom:a24.1: The woman: who is a zava [Rashi and the translation: a menstruating woman], and milk dripped from her nipples and fell into the airspace of an oven: the oven is impure, that is, the food inside it is impure, for the milk is first-degree food, and first-degree food renders second-degree food impure by way of being rendered susceptible. And it poses a difficulty for us: in what way was it rendered susceptible? And Rabbi Yoḥanan said: by the drop, etc. Evidently it is not a spring, and it needs to be rendered susceptible.
gershom:a25.1: And if you say Rava does not hold in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan: [who holds] that it is food and needs to be rendered susceptible; rather, it is a spring.
gershom:a26.1: But isn’t it taught: You are found saying, etc. And ill-smelling pus: that is, his putrid [discharge].
gershom:b1.1: [An editor’s marker notes that what precedes belongs to 13a.] Impart the impurity of liquids with a quarter[-log]: for with regard to all these three, [the word] “drink” [mashkeh] is written.
gershom:b2.1: Severe impurity: by contact and by carrying [hesset].
gershom:b3.1: And if you say milk is a spring, etc.
gershom:b4.1: If so: since you say that it is not a spring, this is difficult: why does it impart impurity even not to satisfaction?
gershom:b5.1: Actually it is not a spring. And do you think that this “not to satisfaction” that it says means where he says he is not agreeable? No; what is “not to satisfaction”? Unspecified. And therefore it imparts impurity even when unspecified, where he did not say that he is agreeable to it, for we hold that when unspecified, his mind is close to the milk; therefore it imparts impurity even unspecified. But if we see that the infant is not agreeable to it, it is not rendered susceptible, and it is pure.
gershom:b6.1: But [if] he ate impure foods and drank impure liquids: it speaks of foods that are a primary source of impurity, having touched a corpse; and where do we find foods that are a primary source of impurity? As it says in the chapter Or LeArba’a Asar. And for these one is liable to karet when he ate them and entered the Temple. [A printed editor’s note: It seems one should read: But [if] he ate impure foods, which is only rabbinic impurity, he is not liable to karet but [violates] a mere prohibition. But for foods impure by rabbinic impurity he is not liable to karet but [violates] a mere prohibition.]
gershom:b7.1: Entered the Temple and remained: this “and remained,” we do not know whether it says he remained in the Temple or remained in eating them.
gershom:b8.1: Rabbi Elazar says: if he interrupted in that quarter[-log], so that he did not drink it all at once, or if he put any amount of water into it and drank it and entered, he is exempt.
gershom:b9.1: Why do I need remaining, that it teaches: [entered the Temple and remained], which implies that it refers to entering the Temple and remaining? But there he needs no remaining at all; rather, once he has entered he is liable. For even there, in tractate Shevuot, where it requires a stay of the measure of a prostration, that applies only where he became impure inside, in the Sanctuary; but where he became impure outside, he is liable immediately when he enters.
gershom:b10.1: Rav Yehuda said: this “and remained” that it teaches refers to his eating.
gershom:b11.1: If so, why does the verse state “wine”? Is it not derived from “intoxicating drink”? To tell you that wine from its press and wine in any amount, they are warned about it: an ordinary prohibition, and not death.
gershom:b12.1: And for other intoxicating drinks, a [mere] prohibition. And for wine, too, in the amount that intoxicates, one is liable to death.
gershom:b13.1: We derive “intoxicating drink,” “intoxicating drink” from a nazirite: as it is written: “He shall abstain from wine and intoxicating drink” (Numbers 6:3). What is “and intoxicating drink” of the nazirite? It speaks of wine and not of other intoxicating drinks.
gershom:b14.1: In accordance with whom? In accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, for he said: and for other intoxicating drinks, a prohibition.
gershom:b15.1: Tuvyana deḥakhimei [“the most gratified of the Sages”]: the best among the Sages, and the halakha follows him.
gershom:b16.1: He came before Rav Ashi: to have his vow dissolved, and it was a Festival.
gershom:b17.1: He said to him: Go now and come tomorrow: for he came before him after eating.
gershom:b18.1: For Rav would not place a disseminator over himself: to expound and to rule on a Festival for the needs of the halakhot of the second Festival day, because of drunkenness, lest he err. And because of drunkenness, too, [Rav Ashi] did not wish to dissolve [the vow] for him until the next day.
gershom:b19.1: Rav Aḥa said to him: But didn’t Rav say: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Elazar, that if he put any amount of water into it he is exempt, since it does not intoxicate?
gershom:b20.1: That is with a quarter[-log]: [the printed text has “in error” in parentheses here] where he drinks only a quarter[-log] and puts any amount of water into it, it does not intoxicate; but if it is more than a quarter[-log], even though he put any amount of water into it, it does not weaken its taste, and it intoxicates; and I drank more than a quarter[-log] of wine.
gershom:b21.1: And that you may differentiate: which is written after “Drink no wine nor intoxicating drink,” teaches that one who has drunk wine should not issue rulings.
gershom:b22.1: Between the sacred and the common: that is, values and valuations and dedications and consecrations: to rule in which manner he [must have] said it for it to be sacred, for if he said it in another manner it is common.
gershom:b23.1: And that you may instruct, this is a ruling: on what is forbidden and permitted.
gershom:b24.1: All the statutes, these are the exposition: that if he expounds aggada in the explanation of verses, he should not explain or rule on them if he has drunk.
gershom:b25.1: Which [the Lord] has spoken, this is halakha [Mishna]: that even with an unattributed mishna he should not engage in order to rule.
gershom:b26.1: By the hand of Moses, this is the Talmud: in which he should not engage at all, for the Talmud explains everything.
gershom:b27.1: One might have thought even Mishna: he should not engage in it, even without intending to rule.
gershom:b28.1: The verse states “and that you may instruct”: it said [this] only of one who studies it in order to rule.
gershom:b29.1: And Rabbi Yosei [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s heading] says: One might have thought that even Talmud he should not study, even without intending to rule.
gershom:b30.1: The verse states “and that you may instruct”: it is forbidden only in order to rule.
gershom:b31.1: Excluded is a creeping animal: that one who has drunk wine may rule on it that it is impure; and likewise on a frog he may rule that one who touches it is pure.
gershom:b32.1: Let us say it is Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda: who permits even Talmud, and not the Rabbis.
gershom:b33.1: You may even say the Rabbis: this is the reason that one may rule on them: for it is [a matter of] “go read it in the schoolhouse” that a creeping animal is impure and not a frog.
gershom:b34.1: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda: that those who have drunk wine are permitted to engage in Talmud.
gershom:b35.1: But Rav would not place a disseminator from one Festival day to the next to explain anything at all in Talmud, because of drunkenness.
gershom:b36.1: Rav is different, for he would issue rulings: for he was accustomed to rule for the public, and if the disseminator explained anything in Talmud before him, it would be impossible that he would not rule.
gershom:b37.1: And let him place [a disseminator] and not rule: that is, let him place a disseminator and guard himself not to rule. This is not feasible, for wherever Rav sat, many people gathered before him and asked him about what is forbidden and permitted, and it was not possible for him without ruling.
gershom:b38.1: Four sin offerings: one because of an impure person who ate sacred [food], one because of forbidden fat, one because of notar, and one because of Yom Kippur; and one guilt offering because of a non-priest [zar] who benefited from consecrated property.
gershom:b39.1: Rabbi Meir says: If it was Shabbat: when he eats and carries it out in his mouth, he is liable to a sin offering because of Shabbat. And even though we say that one who carries out in his mouth, on the back of his hand or with his elbow is exempt, since he did not carry out in the manner of those who carry out, that applies when he carried out his other objects in his mouth; but food [is carried] in its normal manner, and [if] he carried it out in his mouth he is liable. They said to him: It is not of the same category: for it is not in the category of eating, [yet] he said that he is liable; for carrying out is not eating.
